title: Analogy
summary: Analogy questions give you one pair (of words, numbers or letter clusters) and ask you to repeat its relationship on a second pair. CGL typically asks 3-5. The skill is naming the relationship precisely — as a one-line sentence or a shift tuple — and testing every option against it.

subtopics.title: The idea of analogy
subtopics.concept:
An analogy question states one relationship and asks you to repeat it: **A : B :: C : ?** — 'A is to B as C is to what?'. The exam never tests knowledge of A, B or C; it tests whether you can *name the relationship* in one precise sentence and apply it exactly.

The relation must be copied in the **same direction** (A→B, so C→?) and at the **same level of specificity**. If 'Butterfly : Caterpillar' is adult-to-young, the answer must be adult-to-young, not merely 'animal to animal'.

Four families appear in SSC CGL: **word analogy** (meaning-based), **number analogy** (operation-based), **letter analogy** (position/shift-based) and **mixed analogy** (letter-number clusters). Numbers and letters are fully checkable by arithmetic; word pairs must be matched by an exact relation sentence.

tricks.title: Speak the relation as a full sentence before touching the options
tricks.body: Convert 'A : B' into a sentence like 'B is the young one of A' or 'each letter of B is 3 ahead of A'. Then test option pairs against the *same sentence*. Options written to look related but failing one word of the sentence are traps.

example.q:
**Q.** 'Doctor : Hospital' :: ? — (a) Teacher : Student (b) Judge : Court (c) Tailor : Fabric (d) Doctor : Medicine

**Sol.** Sentence: 'the second is the *workplace* of the first'. Teacher : Student is teacher-to-person, Tailor : Fabric is worker-to-material, Doctor : Medicine is worker-to-object. Only **Judge : Court** is professional-to-workplace.
example.solution: Relation sentence kills 3 wrong options in one line — never start by comparing options with each other.

mistakes: Matching the *category* instead of the relation: 'Rose : Flower' and 'Car : Vehicle' are same-category pairs, but 'Rose : Flower :: Car : ?' does not give 'Vehicle' — the relation of the model pair (member to its class) applied to Car would need a class like 'Machine'.
Reversing direction: if 'Chick : Hen' (young→adult) is given, the answer must also be young→adult; 'Hen : Chick' in the options is a trap.
Stopping at the first option that 'sounds related' — options are built so exactly two pairs sound plausible.
subtopics.notes:
### What is an analogy?
An analogy is a comparison of two relationships. In daily life you may say, "a teacher works in a school just as a doctor works in a hospital". Both pairs share one link: *a person and the place where that person works*. In the exam this is written as **Teacher : School :: Doctor : Hospital**. Read the single colon ( : ) as "is to" and the double colon ( :: ) as "as".

The question shows three terms and hides the fourth, or shows one pair and asks you to pick a matching pair. You are **not** tested on how much you know about the words or numbers. You are tested on one skill: can you name the link correctly and copy it without changing it?

### The four-step method
1. **Say the link as one full sentence.** "The second word is the young one of the first." "The second number is the first multiplied by 5." "Each letter moves 2 places forward."
2. **Keep the direction.** If the first pair goes adult → young, the second pair must also go adult → young. Cow : Calf :: Horse : **Foal**, not Horse : Mare.
3. **Apply the same sentence to the third term.** Do not invent a new rule for the second pair.
4. **Test every option.** If two options seem to fit, your sentence is too loose. Make it sharper (add gender, add "measures", add "made from") until only one option survives.

### Kinds of analogy
| Kind | Example | What decides the answer |
|---|---|---|
| Word | Pen : Write :: Knife : Cut | meaning or use |
| Letter | ACE : BDF :: GIK : HJL | alphabet positions |
| Number | 3 : 27 :: 5 : 125 | an arithmetic rule |
| Mixed | C5 : F10 :: H8 : K16 | a letter rule and a number rule |
| Number set | (2, 4, 8) and (3, 9, 27) | one rule joining all three numbers |

### Formats of the question
- **Single blank at the end**: A : B :: C : ? — the most common form.
- **Blank at another place**: ? : B :: C : D or A : ? :: C : D. Find the rule from the complete pair and run it **backwards** if needed. If 5 : 125 is "cube", then ? : 64 means "which number cubed gives 64?" — the answer is 4.
- **Three-term analogy**: A : B : C :: D : E : ? — one rule joins all three terms in order. In 2 : 4 : 8, the terms are 2¹, 2², 2³, so 3 : 9 : ? needs 3³ = 27.
- **Double blank**: A : ? :: ? : D — each option gives two words or numbers. Put both into the blanks and keep the option where both halves follow the same rule.
- **Pair selection**: "Select the pair that is related in the same way as X : Y". Name the link of X : Y and test all four pairs.

### Precision decides close options
Many options come from the same field on purpose. In **Thermometer : Temperature :: Odometer : ?**, the options may be Distance, Speed, Kilometre and Car. All are about vehicles, but the link is "instrument : quantity it measures". An odometer measures **distance**; speed is measured by a speedometer, and a kilometre is only a *unit* of distance. The sharper sentence removes the traps.

### Common traps
- Reversing the direction (young → adult in one pair, adult → young in the other).
- Picking an option only because it is from the same topic (another animal, another number), not because it has the same link.
- Using one rule for the first pair and a slightly different rule for the second pair.
- Stopping at the first option that "looks right" without checking the other three.

### Quick revision
- ":" = is to, "::" = as. The link must be copied exactly, in the same direction.
- Method: name the link in one sentence → apply → test all four options.
- Missing first term? Run the rule backwards (divide instead of multiply, subtract instead of add).
- Three-term: one rule links all three terms in order. Double blank: both halves must use the same rule.
- Two options fit? Sharpen the sentence (gender, unit vs quantity, tool vs product, part vs material).

patterns.name: Missing term in the first or second place (? : B :: C : D)
patterns.howToSpot: The question mark is not at the end, e.g. '? : 64 :: 5 : 125' or 'Dog : ? :: Horse : Neigh'.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the link from the complete pair.
2. Write it as an equation or sentence (B = A³, 'second word is the sound of the first').
3. Run it backwards for the missing term (take the cube root, find the animal that makes the sound).

*Why it works:* the link is the same in both pairs; only the unknown's position has moved.

example.solution: 5 : 125 means 125 = 5³. So ? : 64 needs ?³ = 64, and 4³ = 64. **Answer: 4.**

patterns.name: Close options — choose the exact relation
patterns.howToSpot: All four options come from the same field (all instruments, all family words, all parts of a book). Two or three look right at first sight.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the link as a sharp sentence ('instrument : what it measures', not just 'related to cars').
2. Test each option with that sentence.
3. Reject options that are a unit, a tool, a material or a place when the link needs a quantity, product or whole.

*Why it works:* the setter places same-field traps; only the exact relation survives a precise sentence.

example.solution: Link: instrument : quantity it measures. An odometer measures **distance**. Speed is measured by a speedometer; a kilometre is a unit, not a quantity; a car only carries the odometer. **Answer: Distance.**

patterns.name: Three-term analogy (A : B : C :: D : E : ?)
patterns.howToSpot: Each side has three terms, e.g. '2 : 4 : 8 :: 3 : 9 : ?' or 'ACE : BDF : CEG :: JLN : KMO : ?'.
patterns.logic:
1. Find how the 1st term becomes the 2nd, and how the 2nd becomes the 3rd.
2. Check whether it is one rule (×2, ×2) or a power pattern (a, a², a³).
3. Apply the same two steps to the second group.

*Why it works:* three terms fix the rule more firmly than two, so there is usually only one fit.

example.solution: 2, 4, 8 are 2¹, 2², 2³. So 3, 9, ? must be 3¹, 3², 3³ = 27. (Doubling 9 to get 18 is the trap — 3 → 9 is not doubling.) **Answer: 27.**

patterns.name: Double blank — choose the pair that fills both blanks
patterns.howToSpot: Two question marks, e.g. '? : Calf :: Horse : ?' — each option gives two items.
patterns.logic:
1. Put option 1 into both blanks and read both pairs.
2. Name the link of each pair. Keep the option only if both links are the same and in the same direction.
3. Repeat for the other options (only one survives).

*Why it works:* a wrong pair usually fits one blank well but creates a different link in the other.

example.q: **? : Calf :: Horse : ?** (Cow, Foal) / (Bull, Stable) / (Cow, Mare) / (Goat, Kid)
example.solution: (Cow, Foal): Cow : Calf is adult : young; Horse : Foal is adult : young ✓. (Bull, Stable) mixes young with home; (Cow, Mare) mixes young with female; Goat : Calf is wrong. **Answer: Cow, Foal.**

subtopics.title: Letter / letter-cluster analogy
subtopics.concept:
Here A, B, C are letters or clusters, and the relation is a **letter-position rule**. Convert every letter to its alphabet position (A=1 ... Z=26) and compare positions of B against A. The rule is almost always one of:

1. **Constant shift**: every letter moves +k or −k (e.g. CAT → FDW is +3).
2. **Different shifts per position**: shifts form their own pattern (+1, +2, +3, ...).
3. **Opposite letter (Atbash)**: A↔Z, B↔Y, ... position p becomes 27−p.
4. **Reversal**: the cluster order flips (EAT → TAE), sometimes combined with a shift.

**EJOTY anchor table** — learn these five positions and every shift becomes a ±1 to ±5 jump from a familiar letter:

| Letter | E | J | O | T | Y |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Position | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 |

**Opposite pairs**: A-Z, B-Y, C-X, D-W, E-V, F-U, G-T, H-S, I-R, J-Q, K-P, L-O, M-N.

formulas.name: Shift rule
formulas.note: Q = alphabet position; k is constant for a constant-shift analogy.

formulas.name: Opposite letter
formulas.note: Atbash: A↔Z, M↔N. Two-letter quick check: sum of positions = 27.

formulas.name: Rising shift
formulas.note: Position i gets shift i — common in 4-letter clusters (BDFH from ABCD).

tricks.title: Subtract positions, then copy the shift pattern
tricks.body: Write positions of A under A, positions of B under B, subtract slot by slot. The shift tuple you get (e.g. +3, +3, +3) is the whole question. Apply the same tuple to C and read the answer with EJOTY.

example.solution: One subtraction row is faster than 'feeling' the pattern; shifts never lie.

tricks.title: Spot Atbash by the 27-sum
tricks.body: If corresponding letters of A and B always add to 27 (C=3, X=24 → 27), the rule is opposite letters. Then answer = opposite of each letter of C — no shifting at all.

example.solution: Opposite pairs table A-Z ... M-N applied letter by letter takes 5 seconds.

tricks.title: Reversal check: read B backwards
tricks.body: If B read backwards is a constant shift of A (or of A reversed), the rule is reversal ± shift. Apply: reverse C, then shift by the same k.

example.q:
**Q.** 'DEB' : 'BED' :: 'LAP' : ?

**Sol.** BED is DEB reversed (no shift). So LAP reversed = **PAL**.
example.solution: Only two things can hide in reversal questions: pure reversal, or reversal + fixed shift — test both.

mistakes: Applying the shift to *positions* instead of letters (adding 3 to '26' giving '29' instead of wrapping to C). Positions wrap mod 26.
Ignoring a mixed shift tuple: treating (+1, +2, +3) as 'constant +2' gives wrong cluster; check every slot.
Confusing opposite-letter (Atbash) with a 13-shift: both map A to N? No — Atbash maps A to Z. Verify with the 27-sum before using the table.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a letter analogy?
Here the terms are letters or groups of letters (called *clusters*), such as **CAT : FDW :: PIN : ?**. The link is always a rule about **alphabet positions**. There is no meaning to find — only counting.

### Step 1: turn letters into numbers
Give every letter its place in the alphabet: A = 1, B = 2 ... Z = 26. Counting from A every time is slow, so learn the **EJOTY** anchors:

| Letter | E | J | O | T | Y |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Position | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 |

Now any letter is a small hop from an anchor: R = T − 2 = 18, L = J + 2 = 12, W = Y − 2 = 23.

Also learn the **opposite pairs** (they add up to 27): A-Z, B-Y, C-X, D-W, E-V, F-U, G-T, H-S, I-R, J-Q, K-P, L-O, M-N. A handy memory line: "**G**o **T**o **H**ell **S**ir" gives G-T and H-S.

### Step 2: subtract slot by slot
Write the position of each letter of the first cluster, then of the second cluster, and subtract. The list of changes is called the **shift tuple**. Example: CAT → FDW. C(3)→F(6) is +3, A(1)→D(4) is +3, T(20)→W(23) is +3. Tuple = (+3, +3, +3). Apply it to PIN: P+3 = S, I+3 = L, N+3 = Q → **SLQ**.

### Wrap-around
After Z the alphabet starts again at A. So Y + 3 = B (25 + 3 = 28, and 28 − 26 = 2 = B). Going back from A also wraps: B − 3 = Y (2 − 3 = −1, and −1 + 26 = 25 = Y).

### The rule bank
1. **Constant shift** — every letter moves the same number of places. EHKN : GJMP is +2 on every letter.
2. **Different shift per slot** — the tuple is not flat but has a pattern: (+1, +2, +3, +4) or (+2, −1, +2, −1). Copy the whole tuple exactly.
3. **Opposite letters** — each letter becomes its opposite (position 27 − p). GOLD : TLOW. Spot it when the pairs of letters add up to 27.
4. **Reversal** — the cluster is written backwards (LAMP : PMAL). It may be combined with a shift: RING → reverse GNIR → +1 → HOJS.
5. **Rearrangement** — letters are swapped in pairs (PLAY : LPYA), or each half is reversed (WINTER : NIWRET), or the first and last letters change places.

### How to pick the rule fast
- Read the second cluster backwards first. If you see the first cluster (or it shifted), it is reversal.
- If the second cluster has the **same letters** in a new order, it is rearrangement.
- Check the first pair of letters: do they add to 27? Then test opposite letters.
- Otherwise subtract positions and read the tuple.

### Worked example
**DRIVE : FUMAK :: PLANT : ?** D→F +2, R→U +3, I→M +4, V→A +5 (22 + 5 = 27 → A), E→K +6. Tuple (+2, +3, +4, +5, +6). PLANT: P+2 = R, L+3 = O, A+4 = E, N+5 = S, T+6 = Z → **ROESZ**.

### Quick revision
- EJOTY: E5, J10, O15, T20, Y25. Opposite pairs add to 27.
- Subtract slot by slot; the tuple is the rule; apply the same tuple.
- Past Z subtract 26; before A add 26.
- Same letters, new order → rearrangement. Backwards → reversal (maybe + shift).
- Missing first cluster → run the tuple backwards (subtract instead of add).

patterns.name: Constant shift letter-cluster analogy
patterns.howToSpot: Every letter of the second cluster is the same number of places ahead of (or behind) the matching letter of the first cluster.
patterns.logic:
1. Subtract positions slot by slot (use EJOTY).
2. Confirm the tuple is flat (+k, +k, +k).
3. Add k to every letter of the third cluster, wrapping past Z.

*Why it works:* the whole cluster moves as one block, so one number describes the rule.

example.solution: E→G, H→J, K→M, N→P are all +2. RUXA + 2: R→T, U→W, X→Z, A→C → **TWZC**.

patterns.name: Different shift for each slot (rising or alternating tuple)
patterns.howToSpot: The changes are not equal but form a pattern: +1, +2, +3, +4 or +2, −1, +2, −1.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the full tuple from the first pair.
2. Do not average it or 'correct' it — copy it exactly.
3. Apply slot 1's change to letter 1, slot 2's to letter 2, and so on.

*Why it works:* the rule is attached to the position in the cluster, not to the letter.

patterns.name: Opposite-letter analogy (and opposite + reverse)
patterns.howToSpot: The letters of the first pair add up to 27 (G + T, O + L). Sometimes the opposite cluster is also written backwards.
patterns.logic:
1. Check one pair: position sum 27 means opposite letters.
2. Replace each letter of the third cluster by its opposite (27 − position).
3. If the model cluster was also reversed, reverse your result too.

*Why it works:* opposite letters are a fixed swap table (A-Z, B-Y ... M-N).

example.solution: G(7)+T(20) = 27, so opposite letters. I↔R, R↔I, O↔L, N↔M → **RILM**.

patterns.name: Reversal and reverse-plus-shift analogy
patterns.howToSpot: Reading the second cluster backwards gives the first cluster, or gives it with every letter moved by the same step.
patterns.logic:
1. Reverse the second cluster and compare with the first.
2. Same letters → pure reversal. Every letter off by k → reverse then shift by k.
3. Do the same two steps, in the same order, on the third cluster.

*Why it works:* reversal changes order, the shift changes letters; the two steps are independent.

example.solution: RING backwards = GNIR; +1 on each gives HOJS. BELL backwards = LLEB; +1 → **MMFC**.

patterns.name: Rearrangement analogy (swapped pairs, halves reversed)
patterns.howToSpot: The second cluster uses exactly the same letters as the first, only in a new order.
patterns.logic:
1. Number the letters of the first cluster 1, 2, 3 ...
2. Write the order in which they appear in the second cluster (e.g. 2-1-4-3).
3. Rearrange the third cluster in the same order.

*Why it works:* the rule is a fixed position map, so letter values do not matter.

example.solution: PLAY (1-2-3-4) → LPYA is order 2-1-4-3 (pairs swapped). GIFT in order 2-1-4-3 → **IGTF**.

subtopics.title: Word analogy
subtopics.concept:
Both pairs are meaningful English word pairs; you must find the option whose pair shares the **same relation**, word-for-word. CGL draws from a fixed relation bank — memorise the bank, not individual questions:

| Relation | Example pair |
|---|---|
| worker : workplace | Chef : Kitchen |
| worker : tool | Surgeon : Scalpel |
| adult : young one | Sheep : Lamb |
| male : female | Colt : Filly |
| animal : home | Horse : Stable |
| animal : sound | Owl : Hoot |
| country : currency | Japan : Yen |
| instrument : quantity | Barometer : Pressure |
| part : whole | Chapter : Book |
| product : source | Flour : Wheat |
| study : subject | Zoology : Animals |
| verb : noun of act | See : Sight |

When two options look right, add precision: Foal is any young horse, Colt only a young *male* horse — relation strength decides.

tricks.title: Two-question test on every option
tricks.body: Ask (1) is the option pair the same *type* of relation? (2) is it the same *specific* relation in the same *direction*? An option surviving question 1 usually dies at question 2 — that is where the exam separates candidates.

example.q:
**Q.** 'Author : Novel' :: ? — (a) Poet : Poem (b) Editor : Newspaper (c) Reader : Library (d) Book : Print

**Sol.** Type: creator-to-creation. Editor : Newspaper is editor-to-periodical (edits, doesn't author it); Reader : Library is user-to-place; Book : Print is thing-to-process. Only **Poet : Poem** is creator-to-literary-creation.
example.solution: Write the two-question answers as ticks/crosses; the option with two ticks is the answer.

tricks.title: Gender/age precision check
tricks.body: For animal pairs, decide whether the model pair is (a) adult:young, (b) male:female or (c) male-young:female-young. Options often mix a young-one with a female — only one matches the model exactly.

example.q:
**Q.** 'Drake : Duck' :: ? — (a) Horse : Mare (b) Bull : Ox (c) Ram : Ewe (d) Dog : Pup

**Sol.** Model = male : female of one species. Horse : Mare is species:female; Bull : Ox is not male:female; Dog : Pup is adult:young. **Ram : Ewe** is male:female of sheep.
example.solution: Name the relation with its gender/age tag before reading options.

mistakes: Choosing an option from the same *topic* (both medical) instead of the same *relation* — topics are decoys; relations decide.
Missing the direction: 'Hunger : Food' (cause:remedy) is not 'Food : Hunger'.
Over-reading: adding a condition the pair does not state ('Judge : Court — but a judge also works in chambers'). Take the primary, standard relation.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a word analogy?
You get a pair of meaningful words, like **Chef : Kitchen**, and a third word. You must find the word that has the same link with the third word. The exam uses a small, fixed bank of links again and again. If you learn the bank, most questions become quick.

### The two-question test
For every option ask:
1. **What is the link?** Say it as a sentence: "a chef *works in* a kitchen".
2. **Does the option make the same sentence with the third word?** "A pilot works in a cockpit" ✓. "A pilot flies an aeroplane" ✗ (different link).

### The relation bank
| Link | Examples |
|---|---|
| Worker : tool | Surgeon : Scalpel, Mason : Trowel, Woodcutter : Axe, Tailor : Needle |
| Worker : place of work | Chef : Kitchen, Judge : Court, Scientist : Laboratory |
| Worker : product | Poet : Poem, Cobbler : Shoes, Weaver : Cloth, Composer : Symphony |
| Adult : young one | Cow : Calf, Horse : Foal, Goat : Kid, Deer : Fawn, Frog : Tadpole |
| Animal : sound | Lion : Roar, Donkey : Bray, Frog : Croak, Horse : Neigh, Owl : Hoot |
| Animal : home | Lion : Den, Bee : Hive, Horse : Stable, Dog : Kennel, Pig : Sty |
| Male : female | Lion : Lioness, Peacock : Peahen, Drake : Duck, Ram : Ewe |
| Individual : group | Fish : Shoal, Wolf : Pack, Lion : Pride, Cattle : Herd, Ship : Fleet |
| Country : currency | India : Rupee, Japan : Yen, Thailand : Baht, Bangladesh : Taka |
| Country : capital | Nepal : Kathmandu, Bhutan : Thimphu, Egypt : Cairo, Canada : Ottawa |
| Instrument : quantity measured | Barometer : Pressure, Hygrometer : Humidity, Anemometer : Wind speed |
| Unit : quantity | Newton : Force, Pascal : Pressure, Joule : Energy, Ampere : Current |
| Study : subject | Ornithology : Birds, Ichthyology : Fishes, Entomology : Insects |
| Product : raw material | Glass : Sand, Paper : Wood, Butter : Milk, Jaggery : Sugarcane |
| Part : whole | Petal : Flower, Page : Book, Player : Team |
| Tool : action | Needle : Sew, Spade : Dig, Knife : Cut, Pen : Write |
| Cause : effect | Rain : Flood, Drought : Famine, Virus : Disease |
| Same meaning (synonym) | Begin : Commence, Abandon : Desert |
| Opposite meaning (antonym) | Ancient : Modern, Scarce : Abundant |
| Degree (mild : strong) | Warm : Hot, Breeze : Gale, Smile : Laugh |

### Precision rules
- **Unit vs quantity vs instrument.** Pascal is a unit, pressure is a quantity, barometer is an instrument. Keep the same type on both sides.
- **Tool vs product vs raw material.** For a weaver: loom is the tool, thread is the raw material, cloth is the product.
- **Young vs female.** Foal is a young horse; mare is a female horse. Do not mix them.
- **Degree direction.** Warm : Hot goes mild → strong, so Breeze : **Gale**, not Breeze : Air.
- **Synonym vs antonym.** If the model pair has the same meaning, the answer must have the same meaning, not the opposite.

### Worked example
**Cobbler : Shoes :: Weaver : ?** (Loom / Cloth / Thread / Tailor). Link: a cobbler *makes* shoes — worker : product. A weaver makes **cloth**. Loom is the tool and thread is the raw material, both traps.

### Quick revision
- Say the link as a sentence; test every option with the same sentence.
- Learn the bank: worker (tool / place / product), animal (young / sound / home / group / female), country (currency / capital), instrument or unit : quantity, study : subject, product : material, part : whole, tool : action, cause : effect, synonym, antonym, degree.
- Same field is not enough — the link type must match exactly.
- Keep direction: if the model goes whole → part, the answer must go whole → part.

patterns.name: Worker : tool / workplace / product
patterns.howToSpot: The first word is a person with a job (mason, cobbler, author, pilot).
patterns.logic:
1. Decide which of the three links it is: tool used, place of work, or thing produced.
2. Find the same link for the new worker.
3. Reject options that are one of the other two links (a tool when the model needs a product).

*Why it works:* every worker has a tool, a place and a product — the setter uses the other two as traps.

example.solution: A cobbler makes shoes (worker : product). A weaver makes **cloth**. Loom = tool, thread = raw material. **Answer: Cloth.**

patterns.name: Animal : young one / sound / home / group
patterns.howToSpot: One word is an animal or bird and the other is its baby, its cry, its shelter or its group name.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify which animal fact is being used.
2. Recall the same fact for the new animal.
3. Make sure the option is not a different fact about the same animal (sound instead of home).

*Why it works:* each animal has one standard word for each fact, learnt in school.

example.solution: A den is the lion's home. A bee's home is a **hive**. Honey is its product, swarm its group, buzz its sound. **Answer: Hive.**

patterns.name: Country : currency / capital
patterns.howToSpot: A country is paired with its money or its capital city.
patterns.logic:
1. See whether the model pair is currency or capital.
2. Recall the same for the new country.
3. The other options are real currencies/capitals of other countries — be exact.

*Why it works:* only one option belongs to the given country.

example.solution: Rupee is India's currency. Thailand's currency is the **baht**. Yuan = China, ringgit = Malaysia, dong = Vietnam. **Answer: Baht.**

patterns.name: Instrument or unit : quantity
patterns.howToSpot: A measuring instrument (barometer, hygrometer) or an SI unit (newton, pascal) is paired with what it measures.
patterns.logic:
1. Note the type of each word: instrument, unit or quantity.
2. Keep the same type pattern for the answer.
3. Recall the fact (anemometer → wind speed, pascal → pressure).

*Why it works:* the traps are usually a unit when a quantity is needed, or a nearby quantity.

example.solution: The newton is the unit of force. The pascal is the unit of **pressure**. (Power = watt, energy = joule, current = ampere.) **Answer: Pressure.**

patterns.name: Study : subject, product : raw material, part : whole
patterns.howToSpot: Words like '-logy' sciences, or a finished product and what it is made from, or a small part and the whole thing.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the link: 'is the study of', 'is made from', 'is a part of'.
2. Apply it to the third word.
3. Watch the direction: product → material, not material → product.

*Why it works:* these links have one clear answer each once the direction is fixed.

example.solution: Butter is made from milk (product : raw material). Jaggery is made from **sugarcane** juice. Sugar is another product, not the material. **Answer: Sugarcane.**

patterns.name: Synonym, antonym and degree pairs
patterns.howToSpot: Two ordinary words that mean the same, the opposite, or a milder and stronger form of the same idea.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide: same meaning, opposite meaning, or mild → strong.
2. Find the option with that link to the third word.
3. Reject the option that has the other type (an antonym when a synonym is needed).

*Why it works:* the setter usually places one synonym and one antonym among the options.

example.solution: Hot is a stronger degree of warm. A stronger degree of a breeze is a **gale**. Calm is the opposite; air is just the general word. **Answer: Gale.**

patterns.name: Tool : action and cause : effect
patterns.howToSpot: An object and what it is used to do (needle : sew), or an event and what it leads to (rain : flood).
patterns.logic:
1. Say 'X is used to ...' or 'X leads to ...'.
2. Complete the same sentence for the third word.
3. Reject places, users and materials connected to the object.

*Why it works:* the answer must be an action or a result, which removes noun traps quickly.

example.solution: A needle is used to sew. A spade is used to **dig**. Garden = place, soil = what is dug, farmer = user. **Answer: Dig.**

subtopics.title: Number analogy
subtopics.concept:
A : B gives a numeric operation; repeat it on C. The operation is always simple and always **uniform** — the same expression turns a into b. Rank the usual suspects:

1. **Linear**: b = k·a + r (e.g. ×3 + 2). Most common by far.
2. **Square/cube based**: b = a² ± r, b = a³, (a+1)², a(a+1), etc.
3. **Digit based**: b = (sum of digits) × k ± r, or reversal of digits.
4. **Powers**: b = 2^a ± r or 3^a ± r.

**Uniqueness habit**: one pair (a, b) admits many rules, so the exam keeps distractors away from every *natural* rule. When your computed answer is missing from the options, your rule is wrong — drop to the next suspect, don't force-fit.

formulas.name: Linear rule
formulas.note: Solve k and r mentally from a and b; verify on the pair before applying to c.

formulas.name: Square family
formulas.note: Test squares first when b is close to a².

formulas.name: Digit sum rule
formulas.note: S(a) = digit sum; common when b is much smaller than a.

tricks.title: Size test picks the family instantly
tricks.body: Compare b with a: if b is a few times a → linear; if b ≈ a² → square family; if b is 10-40 → digit rule when a is 2-digit; if b is small with big a → digit sum.

example.solution: Size test → family → one-line arithmetic.

tricks.title: Verify the rule on the model pair before the probe
tricks.body: Whatever rule you guess, check it reproduces b from a exactly. Guessing ×4+1 from 12 : 49 fails instantly (12×4+1 = 49 passes!) — then apply to c. The 2-second check prevents half the errors.

example.solution: Model-pair verification is the cheapest correctness check in the paper.

mistakes: Forcing a rule that ignores the model pair's exact value (fitting 12:49 with ×4+1 is right, but with ×4+0 it is wrong — check!).
Mixing two different rules for the two pairs (using squares for the model and cubes for the probe).
Digit-reversal missed: 27 : 72 looks like ×2+18 but the intended relation is reversal; if reversal reproduces b, prefer it.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a number analogy?
You get a pair like **4 : 20** and a third number, say 7. The first pair hides an arithmetic rule. You apply the same rule to 7. Here 20 = 4 × 5, so 7 × 5 = 35.

### Step 1: the size test
Look at how big the second number is compared with the first. It tells you which family to try first.

| What you see | Family to try first |
|---|---|
| Second number a little bigger | add or subtract, or ×2 ± small number |
| Second number about k times bigger | ×k ± r |
| Second number near the square of the first | a² ± r, a(a + 1), (a + 1)² |
| Second number huge | a³ ± r |
| Two-digit numbers, answer small | digit sum, digit product |
| Digits look swapped | reverse the digits |

### Step 2: know your squares and cubes
Squares 1 to 20: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144, 169, 196, 225, 256, 289, 324, 361, 400.
Cubes 1 to 12: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, 1000, 1331, 1728.
When you see 35, think 36 − 1. When you see 126, think 125 + 1. When you see 72, think 8 × 9 = a(a + 1) for a = 8.

### The rule bank
1. **Linear**: b = k·a ± r. Example 9 : 40 → 9 × 4 + 4 = 40; so 13 → 13 × 4 + 4 = 56.
2. **Square based**: b = a² ± r, a(a + 1), a(a − 1). Example 6 : 35 → 6² − 1; so 9 → 80.
3. **Cube based**: b = a³ ± r. Example 4 : 65 → 4³ + 1; so 5 → 126.
4. **Digit based**: product of digits (47 → 4 × 7 = 28), sum of digits, square of the digit sum (36 → (3 + 6)² = 81), reversed digits (34 → 43).
5. **Chain of pairs**: 4 : 20 :: 6 : 42 :: 8 : ? — two model pairs fix the rule. 4 × 5, 6 × 7, so 8 × 9 = 72.

### Why you must test the rule, and use the options
One pair can fit many rules. 7 : 23 fits 7 × 3 + 2 and also 7 × 2 + 9. For 11 these give 35 and 31. The examiner keeps only one of these answers in the options. So:
- Find the simplest natural rule and compute the answer.
- If your answer is **not** in the options, try the next family. Do not force a rule.
- If two model pairs are given, your rule must fit **both**.

### The whole-number note
Many papers add: "Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking them into digits." When this note is present, do **not** use digit sums or digit products. Only use operations on the full number (×, +, squares, cubes).

### Pair-selection form
"Select the pair in which the numbers are related in the same way as 7 : 49." Find the link (a²), then check all four pairs. Only 9 : 81 keeps the link. Check each pair fully — the traps are near misses like 8 : 60.

### Worked example
**8 : 72 :: 12 : ?** 72 is 8 × 9 = a(a + 1). So 12 × 13 = **156**. Traps: 144 (12², forgot the +a), 132 (12 × 11, used a − 1).

### Quick revision
- Size test first: small change → linear; near a square → a² ± r; huge → cube.
- Know squares to 20 and cubes to 12 by heart.
- Check the rule on the model pair before using it; answer missing → change family.
- Whole-number note present → no digit tricks.
- Pair-selection: one rule, test every pair completely.

patterns.name: Linear rule: b = k × a ± r
patterns.howToSpot: The second number is a few times the first, plus or minus a small number (7 : 23, 9 : 40).
patterns.logic:
1. Divide b by a to guess k (23 ÷ 7 ≈ 3).
2. Find r = b − k·a (23 − 21 = 2).
3. Apply k·c + r to the third number, then check the answer is in the options.

*Why it works:* most setters build number pairs with one multiplication and one small addition.

patterns.name: Square or cube based rule
patterns.howToSpot: The second number is close to a square or cube of the first (6 : 35, 4 : 65, 8 : 72).
patterns.logic:
1. Compare b with a² and a³.
2. Note the difference (35 = 36 − 1; 65 = 64 + 1) or the product form (72 = 8 × 9).
3. Apply the same form to the third number.

*Why it works:* squares and cubes grow fast, so a large jump almost always means a power.

patterns.name: Digit-based rule (sum, product, reversal)
patterns.howToSpot: Two-digit numbers where the second number is small or looks like the digits rearranged (47 : 28, 36 : 81, 34 : 43).
patterns.logic:
1. Try digit product, digit sum and the square of the digit sum.
2. Try reversing the digits.
3. Use this family only when the whole-number note is NOT given.

*Why it works:* digit rules explain pairs that no simple ×k ± r rule can.

example.solution: 4 × 7 = 28 (product of digits). So 5 × 9 = **45**. (14 is the digit sum trap.)

patterns.name: Select the number pair with the same relation
patterns.howToSpot: 'Select the option in which the numbers share the same relationship as 7 : 49' — the options are complete pairs.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the rule of the model pair.
2. Test all four pairs with that rule.
3. If two pairs fit, look for a sharper rule that fits the model and only one option.

*Why it works:* the traps are near misses (off by 1 or 2), which a full calculation catches.

subtopics.title: Number sets (triads) analogy
subtopics.concept: Two or more sets of numbers such as (6, 13, 27) and (8, 17, 35) share one hidden rule; you pick the option set that follows the same rule. The rule links all numbers of a set — a repeated step (×2 + 1), the third made from the first two (a × b, a² + b²), powers (a, a², a³) or a middle number made from the outer two. Most papers add the note that operations must be done on whole numbers, so digit tricks are not allowed.

formulas.name: Chain rule
formulas.tex: b = ka + r,\; c = kb + r

tricks.title: Check the last number first
tricks.body: Build the rule from the model sets, then for each option compute only what the last number should be. Traps nearly always change the last number by 1 to 3, so this finds the answer in one pass.

example.solution: Rule (a, a², a³). Last numbers should be 64, 125, 216, 343. Only (5, 25, 125) matches. **Answer: (5, 25, 125).**

mistakes: Breaking numbers into digits when the question says to use whole numbers only.
Accepting a rule that fits the first model set but not the second.
Checking only the first two numbers of an option and missing that the third is off by one.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a number-set analogy?
This is a newer and very common form. You are shown two or more **sets** of numbers, such as (6, 13, 27) and (8, 17, 35). All numbers inside a set are linked by the same rule. You must pick the option set whose numbers follow **the same rule**.

The question usually carries a note: *"Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits. E.g. 13: operations on 13 such as adding, subtracting or multiplying 13 are allowed; breaking 13 into 1 and 3 is not allowed."* So only use +, −, ×, ÷, squares and cubes of the full numbers. No digit tricks.

### How the rule can be built
There are four families you will meet again and again.

**1. Chain rule (first → second → third).** The same step is used twice. In (6, 13, 27): 6 × 2 + 1 = 13 and 13 × 2 + 1 = 27. Check (8, 17, 35): 8 × 2 + 1 = 17, 17 × 2 + 1 = 35 ✓. The step can also change: (4, 9, 27) is +5 then × 3.

**2. Third from the first two.** The third number is made from the other two: product (3, 8, 24), sum of squares (4, 5, 41 because 16 + 25 = 41), twice the sum (5, 9, 28).

**3. Power sets.** Numbers are powers or near-powers of the first: (2, 4, 8) is a, a², a³; (3, 10, 28) is a, a² + 1, a³ + 1; (7, 49, 56) is a, a², a + a².

**4. Middle links the outer two.** The middle number is made from the two outer numbers: (5, 35, 7) because 5 × 7 = 35; (8, 13, 18) because 13 is the average of 8 and 18. Or the first is the sum of the other two: (14, 5, 9).

### Method
1. Take the first model set. Try the chain rule: how does the 1st become the 2nd? Does the same step turn the 2nd into the 3rd?
2. If not, try the third from the first two: a + b, a × b, a² + b², (a + b) × k.
3. If not, try powers, then the middle-link family.
4. **Confirm the rule on the second model set.** A rule that fits only one set is wrong.
5. Test the four options one by one. Exactly one fits. Traps are usually off by 1 to 3 in the last number.

### Worked example
Sets: (4, 5, 41), (3, 7, 58). Chain? 4 → 5 is +1 but 5 → 41 is not +1. Third from first two: 4² + 5² = 16 + 25 = 41 ✓; 3² + 7² = 9 + 49 = 58 ✓. Options: (2, 6, 40), (5, 4, 40), (6, 3, 36), (1, 8, 64). 2² + 6² = 4 + 36 = 40 ✓; 25 + 16 = 41 ✗; 36 + 9 = 45 ✗; 1 + 64 = 65 ✗. **Answer: (2, 6, 40).**

### Speed tips
- Check the **last number first** in each option — traps usually change only that.
- If the numbers grow about ×2 each step, try ×2 ± 1; about ×3, try ×3 ± 1.
- Numbers like 26, 37, 50, 65 are squares + 1; 28, 65, 126 are cubes + 1.

### Quick revision
- Obey the whole-number note: no digit sums or products.
- Four families: chain (a → b → c), third from first two, power sets, middle links outer.
- The rule must fit every model set before you test options.
- Test all options fully; exactly one follows the rule.

patterns.name: Chain rule sets (a → b → c by the same step)
patterns.howToSpot: In each set the numbers grow step by step: (6, 13, 27), (8, 17, 35).
patterns.formula: b = k a + r,\; c = k b + r
patterns.logic:
1. Find the step from the 1st to the 2nd number (× k ± r or + r).
2. Check the same step takes the 2nd to the 3rd.
3. Confirm on the other model set, then test the options.

*Why it works:* a repeated step is the simplest rule that links three numbers.

example.solution: Rule: × 2 + 1 each step (6 → 13 → 27). (5, 11, 23): 5×2+1 = 11, 11×2+1 = 23 ✓. The others fail at the last number. **Answer: (5, 11, 23).**

patterns.name: Third number from the first two
patterns.howToSpot: The third number is bigger than both and looks like a product, a sum of squares or a multiple of the sum.
patterns.logic:
1. Try a × b, a + b, a² + b², (a + b) × k on the model sets.
2. Keep the one that fits every model set.
3. Apply it to each option's first two numbers and compare with its third.

*Why it works:* the first two numbers are 'inputs' and the third is the 'output'.

example.solution: Rule: third = first × second (3 × 8 = 24, 5 × 6 = 30). 7 × 4 = 28 ✓; 30, 27, 16 fail the others. **Answer: (7, 4, 28).**

patterns.name: Power sets (a, a², a³ and near-powers)
patterns.howToSpot: The second number is the square of the first, the third looks like a cube, or both are 'square + 1' and 'cube + 1'.
patterns.logic:
1. Compare the 2nd number with a² and the 3rd with a³ (or a + a²).
2. Note any ± r.
3. Test each option by building a², a³ from its first number.

*Why it works:* powers grow so fast that they are easy to recognise.

patterns.name: Middle number links the outer two (or first = sum of the others)
patterns.howToSpot: The middle number is the product or the average of the outer two, or the first number equals the sum of the other two.
patterns.logic:
1. Multiply, add and average the outer numbers; compare with the middle.
2. Also test first = second + third.
3. Confirm on all model sets, then test the options.

*Why it works:* setters sometimes hide the 'output' in the middle instead of at the end.

example.solution: Middle = first × third (5 × 7 = 35, 4 × 9 = 36). 6 × 8 = 48 ✓; 27, 63 and 16 fail the others. **Answer: (6, 48, 8).**

subtopics.title: Mixed clusters and same-relation selection
subtopics.concept:
Two CGL variants sit outside the classic three:

1. **Mixed cluster analogy**: A : B :: C : ? where A and B contain both letters and numbers ('B3D : E6J'). Each component follows its own mini-rule (letters shift, number doubles, etc.). Solve component-wise and assemble the answer.
2. **Same-relation selection**: four complete pairs are given; pick the pair whose relation matches a stated model pair (or pick the pair that does NOT belong, when asked). Test all four pairs with the same relation sentence from the model.

For mixed clusters, never solve the cluster as a whole — split by character type and solve each track separately.

tricks.title: Solve tracks, then assemble
tricks.body: In a mixed cluster make one column for letters (positions/shifts) and one for numbers (their own series). Fill the answer character by character — each column is independent, so an error stays inside one column.

example.solution: Component-wise solving turns 1 hard cluster into 2 easy columns.

tricks.title: One sentence for all four pairs
tricks.body: In same-relation selection, form the relation sentence once from the model pair and tick/cross every option against the *same* sentence, in the same order. The first option that passes both halves is the answer.

example.q:
**Q.** 'Sword : Sheath' :: pick the same-relation pair — (a) Rifle : Trigger (b) Knife : Blade (c) Rose : Petal (d) Blade : Cover is not; use (d) Bullet : Barrel

**Sol.** Sentence: 'second is the container/cover of the first when stored'. Trigger, Blade, Petal are parts, not containers. **Bullet : Barrel** — barrel houses the bullet.
example.solution: Container–thing, worker–tool, cause–effect: name the abstract frame, then match frames.

mistakes: Assuming the number track follows the letter track's rule — the two tracks are independent.
In same-relation selection, matching only the first half of the relation (both 'container' pairs) without checking the second half (what is contained).
Missing an embedded digit rule like 'number = position of the first letter' (B3D → 3 is C's position... actually A=1; check the model, don't assume).
subtopics.notes:
### What is a mixed analogy?
Mixed analogies join two worlds: letters and numbers, or words and numbers. The good news is that each part follows its own simple rule. You solve the parts one at a time and then put the answer together.

### Type 1: letter-number clusters
Example: **C5 : F10 :: H8 : ?**
- Letter track: C(3) → F(6) is +3. So H(8) + 3 = K.
- Number track: 5 → 10 is × 2. So 8 × 2 = 16.
- Answer: **K16**.

The two tracks do not affect each other. Solve the letters with positions (EJOTY helps) and the numbers with arithmetic. If a cluster has two letters (B3D), each letter slot has its own shift.

Sometimes the number is built **from** the letter: D16, F36, H64 — each number is the square of its letter's position (D = 4, 4² = 16). Then the next letter decides the number.

### Type 2: word → number
Example: **CAT : 24 :: BAT : ?**
The number comes from the letter positions of the word. The rule bank:
1. **Sum of positions**: CAT = 3 + 1 + 20 = 24.
2. **Sum × k or sum ± r**: DOG = 26, coded as 52 → × 2.
3. **Reverse positions** (A = 26, B = 25 ... Z = 1): each letter counts as 27 − p.
4. **Number of letters** × something (rare).

Work out the sum for the model word first; then compare it with the given number to find the extra step.

### Type 3: letter → number
Example: **C : 9 :: E : ?** C is the 3rd letter and 9 = 3². So E (5th) gives 5² = **25**. Other common rules: 2 × position, reverse position (B → 25), position + constant.

### Type 4: same-relation word pairs
"Select the pair that is related in the same way as Tailor : Needle." Say the link — *worker : tool* — and test all four pairs. Traps are pairs from the same world with a different link: Doctor : Hospital (workplace), Author : Book (product).

### Solving method in short
1. Split the term into its parts (letters, numbers, word, number).
2. Find one small rule per part from the model pair.
3. Apply each rule to the matching part of the third term.
4. Join the parts and look for the exact combination in the options (traps change just one part).

### Common mistakes
- Solving the letter part correctly but copying the wrong number (or the reverse). Options usually differ in only one part.
- Using A = 0 instead of A = 1 when counting positions.
- For word → number, forgetting the extra × k or + r that the model pair revealed.
- In pair selection, choosing a pair from the same topic instead of the same link.

### Quick revision
- Split, solve each track, then join.
- Letter tracks: positions and shifts. Number tracks: +, ×, squares.
- Word → number: first try the plain sum of positions, then × k or ± r.
- Letter → number: position, 2 × position, position², reverse position (27 − p).
- Pair selection: one link sentence tested on all four pairs.

patterns.name: Letter-number cluster analogy
patterns.howToSpot: Terms like 'C5 : F10' or 'P7R : S14U' mix letters and numbers.
patterns.logic:
1. Split each term into a letter track and a number track.
2. Find the letter shift and the number rule separately.
3. Apply both to the third term and join the parts.

*Why it works:* the tracks are independent, so each one is a tiny, easy question.

example.solution: Letters: C → F is +3, so H → K. Numbers: 5 → 10 is × 2, so 8 → 16. **Answer: K16.**

patterns.name: Word to number (sum of letter positions)
patterns.howToSpot: A word is paired with a number, e.g. 'CAT : 24 :: BAT : ?'.
patterns.logic:
1. Add the positions of the model word's letters.
2. Compare the sum with the given number: equal, × k, or ± r.
3. Find the sum for the new word and apply the same extra step.

*Why it works:* setters build the number from letter positions in one or two simple steps.

patterns.name: Select the word pair with the same relation
patterns.howToSpot: A model pair followed by four complete word pairs: 'Select the pair related in the same way as Tailor : Needle'.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the link of the model pair as a sentence.
2. Put each option pair into that sentence.
3. Only one pair should make a true sentence in the same direction.

*Why it works:* traps share the topic but not the link (workplace instead of tool).

example.q: **Tailor : Needle** — (Painter : Brush / Doctor : Hospital / Author : Book / Farmer : Crop)
example.solution: Link: worker : tool used. Painter uses a brush ✓. Hospital = workplace, book and crop = products. **Answer: Painter : Brush.**

patterns.name: Letter to number (position-based)
patterns.howToSpot: A single letter is paired with a number, e.g. 'C : 9 :: E : ?' or 'B : 25 :: D : ?'.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the letter's position (and its reverse position 27 − p).
2. See how the number is built: p², 2p, 27 − p, p + r.
3. Apply the same build to the new letter.

*Why it works:* only a few simple formulas are used, and each is quick to test.

example.solution: C is 3rd and 9 = 3². E is 5th, so 5² = **25**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Letter-cluster analogy with a constant shift
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Three letter clusters and a blank, such as 'EHKN : GJMP :: RUXA : ?'. Every letter of the second cluster is the same number of places away from the first.
pyqPatterns.approach: Write positions using EJOTY, subtract slot by slot and confirm the change is the same everywhere. Add that change to each letter of the third cluster, wrapping past Z.

example.solution: Each letter moves +2 (E→G, H→J, K→M, N→P). RUXA + 2 = **TWZC**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Letter analogy with a per-slot, opposite or reversal rule
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The shift is not the same for every letter, or letters pair to 27 (opposites), or the second cluster read backwards gives the first.
pyqPatterns.approach: Test in this order: backwards reading (reversal), 27-sum (opposites), then the full shift tuple. Copy the discovered rule exactly — the same tuple, the same order of steps.

example.solution: G + T = 27, so letters are replaced by opposites. IRON → **RILM**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Word analogy from the standard relation bank
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A meaningful word pair (Mason : Trowel, Lion : Den, Newton : Force) and a third word with a blank.
pyqPatterns.approach: Say the link as one sentence (worker : tool, animal : home, unit : quantity) and test every option with it. Reject options from the same field that have a different link.

example.solution: The newton is the unit of force; the pascal is the unit of **pressure**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Number analogy with one model pair
pyqPatterns.approach: Use the size test to choose the family (linear, square, cube, digit). Check the rule on the model pair, apply it, and if the answer is missing from the options move to the next family.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Number sets (triads) with a common rule
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two sets like (6, 13, 27) and (8, 17, 35), with the whole-number note; options are sets of three numbers.
pyqPatterns.approach: Try the chain rule, then 'third from the first two', then powers, then the middle-link family. Confirm on both model sets, then compute what each option's last number should be.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Select the pair with the same relation
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A model pair of words or numbers followed by four complete pairs.
pyqPatterns.approach: Write the link of the model pair once and test all four pairs completely. For numbers, compute each pair exactly — traps miss by one or two.

example.q: Select the pair related like **Tailor : Needle**: Painter : Brush / Doctor : Hospital.
example.solution: Worker : tool. A painter uses a brush → **Painter : Brush**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Terms such as 'C5 : F10 :: H8 : ?' or 'RAM : 32 :: SHAM : ?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Split into a letter track and a number track, or compute the sum of letter positions for the word. Find one small rule per part and join the parts.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Blank in another position, three-term and double-blank analogies
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The question mark is in the first or second place, there are three terms per side, or there are two blanks with pair options.
pyqPatterns.approach: Find the rule from the complete pair and run it backwards if the first term is missing. For double blanks, put each option into both places and keep the one where both pairs share the same link.

solvedExamples.q: Select the related letters: **CAT : FDW :: PIN : ?**
solvedExamples.shortcut: Position subtraction row: (+3, +3, +3). Copy the tuple onto the probe — no letter-by-letter guessing.

solvedExamples.q: Select the related word: **Surgeon : Scalpel :: Carpenter : ?**
solvedExamples.solution: Relation: worker to his **cutting tool**. Wood is material, Nail is fastener (not the carpenter's cutting tool), Furniture is product. **Saw** is the carpenter's cutting tool.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Worker-tool pairs: match *what the tool does* — the surgeon's scalpel cuts, the carpenter's saw cuts.
solvedExamples.pattern: word analogy from the standard relation bank

solvedExamples.solution: 4 × 5 = 20 suggests ×5, but 7 × 5 = 35 is absent — so test the next family: 4(4+1) = 20 ✓. Then 7(7+1) = **56**. (49 = 7² is the square trap; the model pair is not 4 : 16.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: When the linear guess (×5) misses the options, try n(n+1) — the second most common number-analogy rule.

solvedExamples.q: Select the related letters: **HE : SV :: GO : ?**
solvedExamples.solution: H(8)+S(19) = 27 and E(5)+V(22) = 27, so the rule is **opposite letters** (Atbash). Opposite of G is T, opposite of O is L → **TL**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Sum 27 confirms Atbash; read the answer straight off the opposite-pairs table A-Z, B-Y, ..., G-T, O-L.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **DOG : GRJ :: CAT : ?**
practice.solution: G−D = +3, R−O = +3, J−G = +3 (positions). The rule is a constant **+3** shift. C(3)+3 = F(6), A(1)+3 = D(4), T(20)+3 = W(23) → **FDW**.
practice.shortcut: One subtraction row gives (+3, +3, +3); add to the probe cluster using EJOTY anchors.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **ABCD : BDFH :: MNOP : ?**
practice.solution: A→B = +1, B→D = +2, C→F = +3, D→H = +4: the shifts themselves rise by 1. Apply (+1, +2, +3, +4) to MNOP: M+1=N, N+2=P, O+3=R, P+4=T → **NPRT**.
practice.shortcut: If constant shift fails, check whether the shift tuple itself is a series (+1,+2,+3,...) — the next most common rule.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **CAT : XZG :: SUN : ?**
practice.shortcut: Position sum 27 = Atbash; convert through the opposite-pairs table in one pass.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **DOT : TOD :: RAT : ?**
practice.solution: TOD is DOT **reversed**. Reversing RAT gives T-A-R → **TAR**.
practice.shortcut: Read the second cluster backwards; if it equals the first (or a constant shift of it), reverse the probe.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **PM : SO :: KY : ?**
practice.shortcut: Per-slot shifts can differ; always subtract slot-wise, never assume one k for all slots.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Sheep : Lamb :: Goat : ?**
practice.solution: Relation: adult animal to its **young one**. The young of a goat is a **kid**. Cub → lion/tiger/bear, Foal → horse, Puppy → dog.
practice.shortcut: Young-ones bank: sheep-lamb, goat-kid, horse-foal, cow-calf, dog-puppy, lion-cub, deer-fawn.
practice.pattern: word analogy from the standard relation bank

practice.q: Select the related word: **Japan : Yen :: Bangladesh : ?**
practice.solution: Relation: country to its **currency**. Bangladesh's currency is the **taka**. Rial → Oman/Saudi Arabia, Dinar → Kuwait/Jordan, Kyat → Myanmar.
practice.shortcut: Currency bank: Japan-yen, Bangladesh-taka, Myanmar-kyat, Mongolia-tugrik, Vietnam-dong.
practice.pattern: word analogy from the standard relation bank

practice.q: Select the related word: **Barometer : Pressure :: Odometer : ?**
practice.solution: Relation: instrument to the quantity it **measures**. An odometer measures **distance** travelled. Speed → speedometer, Temperature → thermometer, Current → ammeter.
practice.shortcut: Instrument bank: barometer-pressure, odometer-distance, sphygmomanometer-blood pressure, hygrometer-humidity.
practice.pattern: word analogy from the standard relation bank

practice.q: Chef : Kitchen — choose the pair with the **same** relation:
practice.solution: Relation: professional to the **place of work**. Judge works in a court ✓. Tailor : Fabric is worker-material, Teacher : Student is worker-person served, Doctor : Medicine is worker-object used.
practice.shortcut: Same-relation selection: test every option against one sentence — 'second is where the first works'.
practice.pattern: select the pair with the same relation

practice.q: Select the related word: **Zoology : Animals :: Entomology : ?**
practice.solution: Relation: branch of study to its **subject**. Entomology is the study of **insects**. (Ornithology → birds, Ichthyology → fishes, Pedology → soil.)
practice.shortcut: Study bank: entomology-insects, ornithology-birds, ichthyology-fishes, etymology-word origins.
practice.pattern: word analogy from the standard relation bank

practice.q: Select the related number: **12 : 26 :: 20 : ?**
practice.solution: 26 = 12 × 2 + 2, so the rule is **double and add 2**. 20 × 2 + 2 = **42**.
practice.shortcut: For two-digit pairs where b ≈ 2a, test 'k·a + r' with small k first; 12×2+2=26 verifies in one line.

practice.q: Select the related number: **2 : 8 :: 3 : ?**
practice.solution: 8 = 2³, so the relation is **cube**. 3³ = **27**. (×4 would give 12 and square-plus-4 gives 13 — neither is offered; the cube reading is the intended, and only surviving, rule.)
practice.shortcut: When b = a² or a³ exactly, the answer is the same power of the probe — 8 and 27 scream cubes.

practice.q: Select the related number: **4 : 20 :: 6 : 42 :: 8 : ?**
practice.shortcut: Two model pairs pin the rule exactly — with n(n+1) confirmed, no other reading competes.

practice.q: Select the related number: **25 : 49 :: 34 : ?**
practice.solution: Digit sum of 25 is 2+5 = 7 and 7² = 49. Digit sum of 34 is 3+4 = 7, and 7² = **49**. Both members share digit sum 7 — the answer is its square again.
practice.shortcut: When a and b look unrelated, compute the digit sum: many CGL analogies are (digit sum)² or (digit sum)×k.

practice.q: Select the related cluster: **B3D : E6G :: H12N : ?**
practice.solution: Letters: B→E and D→G are both **+3** (B=2→5=E, D=4→7=G). Number: 3→6 is **×2**. Apply to H12N: H+3 = K, N+3 = Q, 12×2 = 24 → **K24Q**.
practice.shortcut: Mixed clusters: solve the letter track (+3, +3) and the number track (×2) separately, then assemble.

practice.q: Select the related number: **? : 64 :: 5 : 125**
practice.solution: 5 : 125 is a **cube** pair (5³ = 125). So ? must satisfy ?³ = 64, and 4³ = 64. **Answer: 4.**
practice.shortcut: Blank first: read the rule from the full pair, then run it backwards (cube root here).

practice.q: Select the related word: **? : Bee :: Den : Lion**
practice.solution: A den is the **home** of a lion. The home of a bee is a **hive**. Honey is the product, buzz the sound, swarm the group — all different links.

practice.q: Select the related number: **? : 225 :: 14 : 196**
practice.solution: 196 = 14², so the second number is the **square** of the first. ?² = 225 gives ? = **15**.
practice.shortcut: Run the rule backwards: square root instead of square.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **? : FDW :: DOG : GRJ**
practice.solution: GRJ is DOG with every letter moved **+3** (D→G, O→R, G→J). So ? = FDW moved **−3**: F→C, D→A, W→T → **CAT**.
practice.shortcut: Blank on the left: apply the discovered tuple backwards (subtract 3).

practice.q: Select the related word: **Speedometer : Speed :: Odometer : ?**
practice.solution: Link: instrument : quantity it **measures**. A speedometer measures speed; an odometer measures **distance**. A kilometre is only the unit; the car merely carries the meter.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Hygrometer : Humidity :: Ammeter : ?**
practice.solution: A hygrometer measures humidity, so the link is instrument : quantity measured. An **ammeter measures current**. Voltage goes with a voltmeter and resistance with an ohmmeter; 'electricity' is too vague.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Author : Book :: Cobbler : ?**
practice.solution: An author **produces** a book. A cobbler produces **shoes**. Leather is the raw material and the shop is the workplace — near, but different links.

practice.q: Select the related number: **3 : 9 : 27 :: 5 : 25 : ?**
practice.solution: 3, 9, 27 are 3¹, 3², 3³ — each term is the cube of the first. So 5, 25, ? ends at 5³ = **125**. (Doubling 25 gives 50 — the trap, because 3 → 9 is not doubling.)

practice.q: Select the related letters: **C : F : I :: D : G : ?**
practice.solution: Each side moves **+3** per step: C(3) → F(6) → I(9). So D(4) → G(7) → 4+6 = 10 = **J**.

practice.q: Select the pair that fills both blanks: **? : Calf :: Horse : ?**
practice.solution: Put each option into both blanks. Cow : Calf and Horse : Foal are both **adult : young** ✓. Bull : Calf mixes male with young; Cow : Mare mixes young with female; Goat : Calf is the wrong baby.

practice.q: Select the pair that fills both blanks: **Lion : ? :: ? : Flock**
practice.solution: The missing pair must keep the link **animal : its group** on both sides. Lion : **Pride** ✓ and **Sheep** : Flock ✓. Den is a home, cub a young one, roar a sound — each breaks one side.

practice.q: Select the pair that fills both blanks: **? : Kitten :: Dog : ?**
practice.solution: Both sides must read **adult : young**. Cat : Kitten ✓ and Dog : Puppy ✓. Kennel is a home and bark a sound, so those options break the link.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **EHKN : GJMP :: RUXA : ?**
practice.solution: E→G, H→J, K→M, N→P: every letter moves **+2**. Apply +2 to RUXA: R→T, U→W, X→Z, A→C → **TWZC** (A wraps past Z).
practice.shortcut: Subtract positions slot by slot; a flat tuple means one shift for all letters.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **NKQ : MJP :: TGA : ?**
practice.solution: N→M, K→J, Q→P: every letter moves **−1**. Apply −1 to TGA: T→S, G→F, A→Z (A wraps back) → **SFZ**.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **CFIL : DHLP :: GJMP : ?**
practice.solution: The shifts rise: C+1 = D, F+2 = H, I+3 = L, L+4 = P — tuple (+1, +2, +3, +4). Apply it to GJMP: G+1 = H, J+2 = L, M+3 = P, P+4 = T → **HLPT**.
practice.shortcut: Copy the whole tuple exactly; do not average or 'tidy' it.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **AZBY : BYCX :: CXDW : ?**
practice.solution: A→B is +1, Z→Y is −1, B→C is +1, Y→X is −1: tuple (+1, −1, +1, −1). CXDW: C+1 = D, X−1 = W, D+1 = E, W−1 = V → **DWEV**.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **GOLD : TLOW :: IRON : ?**
practice.solution: G(7) + T(20) = 27, so each letter is replaced by its **opposite** (27 − position). I↔R, R↔I, O↔L, N↔M → **RILM**.
practice.shortcut: Letter pairs adding to 27 mean the opposite-letter table (A-Z, B-Y ... M-N).

practice.q: Select the related letters: **CA : XZ :: GE : ?**
Select the related letters: **RING : HOJS :: BELL : ?**
practice.solution: RING backwards is GNIR, and +1 on each gives HOJS — **reverse, then shift**. BELL backwards is LLEB; +1 on each → **MMFC**.
practice.shortcut: Read the second cluster backwards first; if it nearly matches, it is reverse (+ shift).

practice.q: Select the related letters: **FLOW : WOLF :: TIME : ?**
practice.solution: WOLF is FLOW **written backwards** — a pure reversal. So TIME reversed is **EMIT**.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **PLAY : LPYA :: GIFT : ?**
practice.solution: PLAY (positions 1-2-3-4) becomes LPYA — the order is **2-1-4-3** (pairs swapped). GIFT in the same order: I, G, T, F → **IGTF**.

practice.q: Select the related letters: **WINTER : RETNIW :: SUMMER : ?**
practice.solution: RETTIW-style check: WINTER written backwards is RETNIW — **pure reversal**. SUMMER backwards is **REMMUS**.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Mason : Trowel :: Woodcutter : ?**
practice.solution: A mason **uses** a trowel — worker : tool. A woodcutter uses an **axe**. Forest is the workplace, wood and tree are what he works on.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Poet : Poem :: Composer : ?**
practice.solution: A poet **creates** a poem — worker : product. A composer creates a **symphony**. The piano is an instrument, an orchestra a group of players, and a musician is a fellow worker.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Donkey : Bray :: Frog : ?**
practice.solution: Bray is the **sound** of a donkey. The sound of a frog is a **croak**. Leap is its action, pond its home, tadpole its young one.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Fish : Shoal :: Wolf : ?**
practice.solution: A shoal is the **group** of fish. The group of wolves is a **pack**. Kennel is a home, howl a sound, cub a young one.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Nepal : Kathmandu :: Bhutan : ?**
practice.solution: Kathmandu is the **capital** of Nepal. The capital of Bhutan is **Thimphu**. Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh, Colombo of Sri Lanka, Naypyidaw of Myanmar.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Japan : Yen :: Thailand : ?**
practice.solution: The yen is the **currency** of Japan. Thailand's currency is the **baht**. Yuan = China, ringgit = Malaysia, dong = Vietnam.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Barometer : Pressure :: Anemometer : ?**
practice.solution: A barometer measures **pressure** — instrument : quantity. An anemometer measures **wind speed**. Humidity goes with a hygrometer and temperature with a thermometer.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Joule : Energy :: Ampere : ?**
practice.solution: The joule is the **unit of energy**. The ampere is the unit of **electric current**. Power is the watt, voltage the volt, resistance the ohm.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Ornithology : Birds :: Ichthyology : ?**
practice.solution: Ornithology is the **study of** birds. Ichthyology is the study of **fishes**. Insects come under entomology.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Paper : Wood :: Glass : ?**
practice.solution: Paper is **made from** wood — product : raw material. Glass is made from **sand** (melted with other minerals).

practice.q: Select the related word: **Ancient : Modern :: Abundant : ?**
practice.solution: Modern is the **opposite** of ancient. The opposite of abundant (plentiful) is **scarce**. Plentiful, copious and rich are synonyms of abundant — the wrong direction.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Begin : Commence :: End : ?**
practice.solution: Commence **means the same as** begin — a synonym pair. A synonym of end is **conclude**. Start, initiate and open go the other way.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Spade : Dig :: Knife : ?**
practice.solution: A spade is **used to** dig — tool : action. A knife is used to **cut**. Kitchen is a place, sharp a quality, chef a user.

practice.q: Select the related word: **Drought : Famine :: Rain : ?**
practice.solution: A drought **leads to** famine — cause : effect. Heavy rain leads to a **flood**. Crops and rivers are affected objects, monsoon is the season.

practice.q: Select the related number: **9 : 40 :: 13 : ?**
Select the related number: **7 : 23 :: 11 : ?**
practice.shortcut: Divide the second number by the first to guess the multiplier; the small leftover is the add-on.

practice.q: Select the related number: **6 : 35 :: 9 : ?**
practice.solution: 35 = 36 − 1 = 6² − 1, so the rule is **square then minus 1**. 9² − 1 = **80**. (81 is the plain-square trap.)

practice.q: Select the related number: **4 : 65 :: 6 : ?**
practice.solution: 65 = 64 + 1 = 4³ + 1, so the rule is **cube then plus 1**. 6³ + 1 = **217**. (216 is the plain cube.)

practice.q: Select the related number: **47 : 28 :: 59 : ?**
practice.solution: 28 = 4 × 7 — the **product of the digits**. For 59: 5 × 9 = **45**. (14 is the digit sum trap.)

practice.q: Select the related number: **36 : 81 :: 45 : ?**
practice.solution: The digit sum of 36 is 9, and 9² = 81 — **square of the digit sum**. Digit sum of 45 is 9, so 9² = **81**.

practice.q: Select the pair in which the numbers are related in the same way as **13 : 41**.
practice.solution: 41 = 13 × 3 + 2. Test each pair with **×3 + 2**: 17 × 3 + 2 = 53 ✓. The others give 47, 59 and 65 — each misses by a few. **Answer: (17, 53).**

practice.q: Select the pair in which the numbers are related in the same way as **8 : 72**.
Select the related cluster: **C5 : F10 :: H8 : ?**
practice.solution: Letter track: C → F is **+3**, so H → K. Number track: 5 → 10 is **×2**, so 8 → 16. Join: **K16**.
practice.shortcut: Solve the letter shift and the number rule separately, then assemble.

practice.q: Select the related cluster: **P7R : S14U :: T5V : ?**
practice.solution: Letters: P → S and R → U are **+3**, so T → W and V → Y. Number: 7 → 14 is **×2**, so 5 → 10. Join: **W10Y**.

practice.q: Select the related cluster: **D16 : F36 :: H64 : ?**
practice.solution: The number is the **square of the letter's position**: D = 4 → 16, F = 6 → 36, H = 8 → 64. Next: J = 10 → 10² = 100 → **J100**.

practice.q: Select the related number: **RAM : 32 :: SHAM : ?**
practice.solution: R + A + M = 18 + 1 + 13 = 32 — the plain **sum of letter positions**. SHAM = 19 + 8 + 1 + 13 = **41**.

practice.q: Select the related number: **CAT : 24 :: PIN : ?**
Select the related number: **DOG : 52 :: COW : ?**
practice.solution: D + O + G = 4 + 15 + 7 = 26, and 26 × 2 = 52 — **sum of positions, doubled**. COW: 3 + 15 + 23 = 41, doubled = **82**. (41 alone is the trap.)

practice.q: Choose the pair related in the same way as **Tailor : Needle**.
practice.solution: A tailor **uses** a needle — worker : tool. A painter uses a **brush** ✓. Hospital is a workplace; book and crop are products.

practice.q: Choose the pair related in the same way as **Lion : Den**.
practice.solution: A den is the **home** of a lion. The home of a bee is a **hive** ✓. Roar and neigh are sounds; puppy is a young one.

practice.q: Choose the pair related in the same way as **Cow : Calf**.
practice.solution: A calf is the **young one** of a cow. The young one of a deer is a **fawn** ✓. Mare is the female (not the baby), wool a product, bleat a sound.

practice.q: Select the related number: **C : 9 :: E : ?**
practice.solution: C is the 3rd letter and 9 = 3² — **square of the position**. E is 5th, so 5² = **25**.

practice.q: Select the related number: **B : 25 :: D : ?**
practice.solution: B(2) pairs with 25 = 27 − 2 — the **reverse position** (Z = 1, Y = 2 ...). D is 4th, so 27 − 4 = **23**.
practice.shortcut: Letter counts down while the number counts up? Try 27 − position.

practice.q: Select the related number: **A : 2 :: D : ?**
practice.solution: A is 1st and 2 = 2 × 1 — **twice the position**. D is 4th, so 2 × 4 = **8**.

practice.q: Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(6, 13, 27)** and **(8, 17, 35)**
Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(3, 5, 9)** and **(5, 9, 17)**
practice.solution: Rule: **×2 then −1** each step — 3 → 5 → 9 and 5 → 9 → 17. Test: 4 → 7 → 13 ✓. The others break at the second or third number (4×2−1 = 7 ≠ 8; 11×2−1 = 21 ≠ 20; 9×2−1 = 17 ≠ 18). **Answer: (4, 7, 13).**

practice.q: Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(2, 6, 18)** and **(4, 12, 36)**
practice.solution: Rule: **×3** each step — 2 → 6 → 18 and 4 → 12 → 36. Test: 5 → 15 → 45 ✓. The others fail at the third number (27, 54, 63 needed). **Answer: (5, 15, 45).**

practice.q: Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(3, 8, 24)** and **(5, 6, 30)**
practice.solution: Rule: **third = first × second** — 3 × 8 = 24 and 5 × 6 = 30. Test: 7 × 4 = 28 ✓. The others give 30, 27 and 16 — not 32, 36, 18. **Answer: (7, 4, 28).**

practice.q: Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(4, 5, 41)** and **(3, 7, 58)**
practice.solution: Rule: **third = a² + b²** — 16 + 25 = 41 and 9 + 49 = 58. Test: 4 + 36 = 40 ✓. The others give 41, 45 and 65. **Answer: (2, 6, 40).**

practice.q: Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(5, 9, 28)** and **(6, 8, 28)**
practice.solution: Rule: **third = 2 × (first + second)** — 2 × 14 = 28 in both sets. Test: 2 × 10 = 20 ✓. The others need 20, 28 and 28. **Answer: (3, 7, 20).**

practice.q: Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(3, 10, 28)** and **(4, 17, 65)**
Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(2, 4, 8)** and **(3, 9, 27)**
Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(7, 49, 56)** and **(5, 25, 30)**
practice.solution: Rule: **(a, a², a + a²)** — 7, 49, 7 + 49 = 56 and 5, 25, 5 + 25 = 30. Test: 6, 36, 6 + 36 = 42 ✓. The others would need 20, 72 and 12 as last terms. **Answer: (6, 36, 42).**

practice.q: Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(5, 35, 7)** and **(4, 36, 9)**
practice.solution: The **middle number = first × third**: 5 × 7 = 35 and 4 × 9 = 36. Test: 6 × 8 = 48 ✓. The others need 27, 63 and 16 in the middle. **Answer: (6, 48, 8).**

practice.q: Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(8, 13, 18)** and **(5, 11, 16)**
practice.solution: The **middle number is the average of the outer two**: (8 + 18)/2 = 13 and (5 + 16)/2 = 11. Test: (6 + 18)/2 = 12 ✓. The others give averages 9.5, 10.5 and 14.5. **Answer: (6, 12, 18).**

practice.q: Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as the numbers of the following sets. (Operations on whole numbers only.) **(14, 5, 9)** and **(20, 8, 12)**
practice.solution: The **first number = second + third**: 5 + 9 = 14 and 8 + 12 = 20. Test: 9 + 8 = 17 ✓. The others give 16, 11 and 24. **Answer: (17, 9, 8).**
